extent:
WHAT THIS SLICE CLAIMS.

- THE ROMAN LINE, from the Council of Trent's two acts touching the Mass through
  Quo primum and its successors to the emended reprint of 2008. The 1570-1962
  stretch is inherited from the base slice and not restated.
- THE ORDINARY OF THE MASS, sixteen units of the Ordo Missae, entering at the
  1962 typical edition because that is the earliest witness in this corpus whose
  text layer carries them, and departing at the 1970 typical edition.
- THE ACTS GOVERNING WHICH MISSAL MAY BE USED, 1984 to 2023, as their own line.
- FIFTEEN FURTHER LINES for uses and order rites, carried as `printed` stations
  where a book survives and as `promulgated` stations where an instrument was
  read.

WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM, and this list is longer than the one above.

- IT CLAIMS NO UNIT OF ANY USE. Not one prayer of Sarum, the Ambrosian, the
  Mozarabic, the Dominican or any other line below has been read into a base
  unit here. Those lines carry their stations, their witnesses and their
  descent, and no liturgy at all. `commonality` therefore reports, correctly,
  that they share no text with the Roman line -- which measures what this file
  holds and NOT what the rites hold. See `commonality_reading`.
- It does not claim the Ordinary before 1962 or after 1970 beyond the departures
  recorded, nor the Canon, nor the chants, nor the lectionary, which after 1969
  is a separate book from the Missal.
- It claims no pre-Tridentine descent for anything. Every pre-1570 line begins
  at a root.
- It does not cover the Eastern Catholic books. The missal acquisition audit
  scopes them separately and says why a Roman-shaped row about an Eastern book
  is a reference that will resolve successfully and wrongly.
- It takes no position on whether any rite or edition is preferable to any
  other. guidance/editorial.md, `No side in what is described`.

Silence here is silence because nothing was established, never because a thing
was checked and found absent. guidance/recensions.md Rule 4.

lines.amends:
The label and note are widened, because this slice carries the line from the
Council of Trent to 2008 rather than from 1570 to 1962. Nothing about the twelve
inherited acts changes.
lines.label: The Roman line: Tridentine mandate, typical editions, postconciliar editions
lines.note:
One line, from the Council of Trent's decree committing the missal to the Roman
Pontiff to the emended reprint of 2008. It is drawn as ONE line and not two
because every act on it names its predecessor or stands in its sequence, and
because the constitution of 1969 opens by reciting Quo primum and Pius V's
promulgation of 1570 in its first sentence, with a footnote citing the bull by
title and date. Whether the rite after 1969 is the same rite is a question this
file does not answer and does not need to: the line records descent of
authority, and the departures record what changed.

lines.amends:
The note said this branch held no witness for any exempted use and was
`honestly empty`. It is no longer empty: fourteen lines below carry printings
and instruments of those uses. The note is rewritten and the superseded sentence
is quoted inside it, so the change is legible rather than invisible.
lines.label: The exempting clause of Quo primum
lines.note:
Quo primum did not abolish every other use. It excepted those whose institution
was approved by the Apostolic See or whose custom had been kept above two
hundred years, and said of them in terms that it took their manner of
celebrating away by no means.

THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS NOTE ENDED: `This tracer holds no witness for any of
them, so the line has its birth act and nothing after it. An empty branch that
is honestly empty is the point.` That was true of the Holy Week slice and is no
longer true of this one.

The clause is still a line of ONE act, and deliberately. It is the legal fact
that the other uses were not abolished; it is not their ancestor. Not one of the
lines below descends from it, because Quo primum did not give those rites
anything -- it declined to take them away, and several of them are three
centuries older than it. Drawing an edge from this clause into the Dominican or
the Ambrosian line would assert a derivation in exactly the direction history
did not run.

lines.label: The acts governing use of the 1962 Missal after 1970
lines.note:
A line born at an act, as every line here is. It carries the instruments
regulating whether and how the 1962 typical edition may still be used after the
Missal of Paul VI: the indult of 1984, Ecclesia Dei, Summorum Pontificum,
Universae Ecclesiae, Traditionis custodes, the Responsa and the rescript of
2023.

It forks from `editio-typica-1962` and never rejoins the Roman line, and the
reason is the rule rather than a judgement: these acts do not revise the Missal
of Paul VI, and the acts on that line do not revise these. They run beside each
other. Whether the two are one rite in two forms or two rites is precisely what
the documents on this line disagree about between 2007 and 2021, and a merge
would assert an answer.

NOTHING ON THIS LINE CARRIES A DEPARTURE. These are acts about which book may be
used, not acts that change a text, and the line's whole content is its stations.

lines.label: Printed missals of the Roman use before Trent
lines.note:
Printings of the Missale Romanum -- the use of the Roman curia -- from before
the Tridentine reform. Every station on this line is `printed`: no act has been
located for any of them, and each is here because the book survives and is
whole.

It is a line and not a heap because each of these books declares itself a missal
of the ROMAN use on its own title page, which is the only thing the edges
assert. It is not a claim that any of them was set from its predecessor. It ends
before Quo primum and does not run into it: the 1570 book was made, on its own
account, by collating ancient codices of the Vatican Library, not by revising
the printing of 1561.

lines.label: The use of Sarum
lines.note:
The English secular use of Salisbury, in its printed tradition. Every station is
`printed`, and `is_typical_edition` never applies: the acquisition audit
establishes that Sarum is a diocesan use with no master general, no general
chapter and no book any authority declared normative, and that its printed
tradition is a commercial one supplied by Rouen, Paris and London printers.
Calling one of them typical would be inventing an authority.

lines.label: The use of York
lines.note: The English secular use of York, in one early printing and one critical edition. No instrument located.

lines.label: The Ambrosian rite of Milan
lines.note:
The largest surviving non-Roman Latin rite. Carried as printed stations only:
the acquisition audit reports promulgating instruments for the 1976, 1981 and
2024 editions from the books' own front matter and from a signed decree, none of
which was read here, so none is asserted.

lines.label: The Hispano-Mozarabic rite
lines.note: The old Spanish rite as printed from the Cisneros edition of 1500 onward. No instrument read here.

lines.label: The rite of Braga
lines.note:
The only line in this file other than the Roman one carrying BOTH a printing and
its own promulgating instruments. Braga's typical edition of 1924 was approved
by a bull of Pius XI and declared typical by a decree of the Sacred Congregation
of Rites, subscribed by the same two officials who signed the Roman typical
edition's decree four years earlier -- which is why the generalisation that the
diocesan uses legislate for themselves is false.

lines.label: The Lyonnais use
lines.note: The use of the primatial church of Lyon. Its printings are at the Bibliotheque nationale de France, which was not reachable from this run.

lines.label: The use of Aquileia
lines.note: A patriarchal use of north-eastern Italy. Two whole printings located; no instrument.

lines.label: The Dominican rite
lines.note:
The rite of the Order of Preachers. The best-documented exempt use in this file:
its early printings are whole and publishable, and from 1604 its promulgating
authority is printed on the title page, which makes a station promulgated rather
than printed at no cost beyond reading a catalogue record.

lines.label: The Carmelite rite, of the use of the Holy Sepulchre
lines.note:
The rite of the Carmelites, which the order's own title page of 1574 describes
as conformed to the norm and custom of the Church of Jerusalem. The Jerusalem
claim is the book's, not a modern gloss.

lines.label: The Carthusian rite
lines.note:
The rite of the Charterhouse. It has the clearest promulgating instrument of any
use in this file -- a general chapter of 1677, named on the title page of the
1679 printing -- and it is also the use this project came closest to writing off
as unavailable. See `[[corrections]]`.

lines.label: The Premonstratensian rite
lines.note: The rite of the Norbertines. Three early printings at the Bavarian State Library, none on the Internet Archive; no instrument read here.

lines.label: The Roman rite in Old Church Slavonic, in the Glagolitic alphabet
lines.note:
NOT A USE EXEMPTED BY QUO PRIMUM, and it is here to show that the eventual scope
has members a search for Latin titles will never return. This is the ROMAN rite,
printed by the Vatican Polyglot Press, in Old Church Slavonic and in the
Glagolitic script. It is drawn as its own line and not as part of the Roman one
because no act joining them was read here; the papal concessions behind it are
reported in the acquisition audit and were not read.

lines.label: The Benedictine monastic missal
lines.note: One printing, of the Cassinese congregation. Carried so the monastic books are not silently absent; nothing more is claimed.
